intro: These adverbs announce the shape of the sentence before it arrives. Each one opens a frame (a guess, an impression, a wish, a supposition, a concession, a comparison, a precious chance) and the sentence must close that frame with the matching ending: きっと ... だろう, どうやら ... らしい, ぜひ ... たい, もし ... たら, たとえ ... ても, まるで ... ようだ, せっかく ... のに. Learn them as pairs, adverb plus ending, and pick the adverb from the ending you hear coming.

skills.rule: To give your own guess about what is or will be true, use きっと (I'm sure), たぶん (probably) or おそらく (probably, formal) and end with だろう / でしょう or と思う.
skills.explain:
All three are the speaker's own judgement, not a report of evidence. They differ in strength and register. きっと is strong conviction, close to 'surely'. たぶん is the everyday 'probably', fine with friends and colleagues alike. おそらく is about as sure as たぶん but sounds formal or written, and is common in news, reports and careful explanations, often about unwelcome outcomes.

The usual ending is だろう / でしょう, or と思う. たぶん and おそらく also sit happily with negatives: たぶん来ないでしょう.

The edge: たぶん and おそらく only guess, so they never go with requests or invitations. きっと can, because it also means 'without fail': きっと来てね (be sure to come). Do not pair きっと with かもしれない; a near-certainty and a maybe contradict each other. For a mere possibility use もしかしたら ... かもしれない.
patterns: きっと [prediction] だろう / でしょう
たぶん [guess] と思う / でしょう
おそらく [formal guess] だろう
きっと [verb] てね / てください (be sure to)

examples.jp: 明日[あした]は{きっと}晴[は]れるでしょう。
examples.en: It will surely be sunny tomorrow.

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さんは{たぶん}来[こ]ないと思[おも]います。
examples.en: I think Ms Tanaka probably won't come.

examples.jp: 君[きみ]なら{きっと}合格[ごうかく]できるよ。
examples.en: You'll pass, I'm sure of it.

examples.jp: この時間[じかん]なら、店[みせ]は{たぶん}もう閉[し]まっているだろう。
examples.en: At this hour the shop has probably already closed.

examples.jp: 犯人[はんにん]は{おそらく}窓[まど]から入[はい]ったのでしょう。
examples.en: The culprit probably came in through the window.

contrast.note: ぜひ expresses a wish or an invitation (ぜひ来てください), not a guess. If the sentence ends in たい or ください, it is ぜひ territory; if it ends in だろう, it is きっと / たぶん.
まさか expresses disbelief and expects a negative: まさか彼が犯人ではないだろう (surely he isn't the culprit). きっと expects the positive.
どうやら ... らしい / ようだ reports what the evidence suggests; きっと ... だろう is your own conviction. Evidence you can point to plus らしい means どうやら.

mistakes.note: たぶん only guesses; it cannot go with a request. Use きっと (be sure to) or ぜひ (I'd love you to).

mistakes.bad: {きっと}雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るかもしれない。
mistakes.good: もしかしたら雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るかもしれない。
mistakes.note: きっと claims near-certainty and かもしれない says 'maybe'. Pair かもしれない with もしかしたら.

skills.tip: Ending in だろう / と思う? It's a guess: きっと if you're sure, たぶん if you're not, おそらく if you're writing.

skills.rule: When you infer something from what you see, hear or feel, use どうやら (by the look of it) or どうも (somehow, it seems) and end with らしい, ようだ or みたいだ.
skills.explain:
These two mark a conclusion drawn from evidence, not a free guess. どうやら is 'by all appearances, it turns out': you have looked at the signs and they point one way, often to something that has finally become clear. どうやら道を間違えたようだ (it looks like we took a wrong turn).

どうも is vaguer: an impression you cannot quite pin down, often that something is off. どうも風邪をひいたみたいだ (I seem to be coming down with a cold). With a negative, どうも also means 'just somehow won't': どうもうまくいかない. This is separate from どうも as 'thanks'.

The edge: both close with an evidential ending, らしい, ようだ, みたいだ (or そうだ for appearance). They clash with だろう / でしょう, which belong to きっと and たぶん, and with wishes and requests, which belong to ぜひ.
patterns: どうやら [conclusion from signs] ようだ / らしい
どうも [vague impression] みたいだ / ようだ
どうも [verb negative] (just won't)

examples.jp: {どうやら}道[みち]を間違[まちが]えたようです。
examples.en: It looks like we've taken a wrong turn.

examples.jp: {どうも}風邪[かぜ]をひいたみたいだ。
examples.en: I seem to have caught a cold.

examples.jp: 隣[となり]の部屋[へや]には{どうやら}誰[だれ]もいないらしい。
examples.en: Apparently there's nobody in the room next door.

examples.jp: 山田[やまだ]さんは最近[さいきん]{どうも}元気[げんき]がないようだ。
examples.en: For some reason Mr Yamada hasn't seemed himself lately.

examples.jp: 聞[き]いた話[はなし]では、{どうやら}会議[かいぎ]は中止[ちゅうし]になったらしい。
examples.en: From what I hear, it seems the meeting has been cancelled.

contrast.note: きっと ... だろう is your own confident prediction. どうやら ... らしい says the signs point that way. Same fact, different source: conviction against evidence.
まるで ... ようだ is a simile: it is like X, but it is not X. どうやら ... ようだ is an inference: it really seems to be X.
ぜひ carries a wish (たい, ください). どうも / どうやら never introduce a wish or a request.

mistakes.bad: {どうやら}彼[かれ]は来[こ]ないでしょう。
mistakes.good: {どうやら}彼[かれ]は来[こ]ないようです。
mistakes.note: どうやら reports what the signs show, so it closes with ようだ / らしい, not with the guessing でしょう.

mistakes.bad: {どうやら}夢[ゆめ]のように楽[たの]しい一日[いちにち]だった。
mistakes.good: {まるで}夢[ゆめ]のように楽[たの]しい一日[いちにち]だった。
mistakes.note: 'A day as fun as a dream' is a simile, not an inference. Similes take まるで.

skills.tip: Can you point at the clue? Then it's どうやら / どうも with らしい or ようだ.

skills.rule: Use ぜひ with your own strong wish (たい) or an eager invitation (てください), どうか with an earnest plea, and どうぞ when you offer something or give permission.
skills.explain:
ぜひ means 'by all means, really'. It strengthens a positive wish or recommendation: ぜひ行きたい, ぜひ食べてみてください, ぜひ一緒に行きましょう. It does not go with negative requests (ないでください) and never with a guess.

どうか is a plea. You ask for something you cannot make happen yourself and you really need: どうか助けてください, どうか許してください. Alone with your own hope it becomes a prayer: どうか合格できますように.

どうぞ hands something to the listener: an offer, a permission, a 'go ahead'. どうぞ座ってください (please, have a seat), どうぞお入りください, and the fixed どうぞよろしくお願いします. どうぞ is about the listener's benefit, so it never goes with your own たい.

So: you want it, ぜひ. You beg for it, どうか. You offer it, どうぞ.
patterns: ぜひ [verb] たい / てみたい
ぜひ [verb] てください / ましょう
どうか [verb] てください / ますように
どうぞ [verb] てください / お [verb] ください

examples.jp: {どうぞ}座[すわ]ってください。
examples.en: Please, have a seat.

examples.jp: 一度[いちど]{ぜひ}京都[きょうと]に行[い]ってみたいです。
examples.en: I'd really love to go to Kyoto at least once.

examples.jp: 日本[にほん]に来[き]たら、{ぜひ}うちに遊[あそ]びに来[き]てください。
examples.en: When you come to Japan, you must come and visit us.

examples.jp: {どうぞ}よろしくお願[ねが]いします。
examples.en: I look forward to working with you.

examples.jp: {どうか}息子[むすこ]を助[たす]けてください。
examples.en: Please, I beg you, save my son.

examples.jp: {どうか}試験[しけん]に合格[ごうかく]できますように。
examples.en: Please let me pass the exam.

contrast.note: たぶん guesses (たぶん来るだろう). It cannot go with たい or ください. A wish or a request takes ぜひ / どうか.
きっと来てね means 'make sure you come'; ぜひ来てね means 'I'd love you to come'. One insists, the other invites.
どうも introduces an impression (どうも調子が悪い) or is a bare 'thanks'. It does not strengthen a wish or a request.

mistakes.note: どうぞ offers or permits something to the listener; it never expresses your own wish. Your own たい takes ぜひ.

mistakes.bad: {ぜひ}遅[おく]れないでください。
mistakes.good: 絶対[ぜったい]に遅[おく]れないでください。
mistakes.note: ぜひ only strengthens doing something; for 'don't do X' use 絶対に.

skills.tip: Want it: ぜひ. Beg for it: どうか. Offer it: どうぞ.

skills.rule: Open a supposition with もし (if), 万一 (if by any chance, for unwelcome events) or 仮に (supposing, for argument's sake) and close it with たら, ば or なら.
skills.explain:
In Japanese the conditional ending does the real work; もし only flags early that an 'if' is coming. It cannot make a clause conditional by itself: the verb must still become 降ったら, あれば, 行くなら. Forgetting the ending after もし is the most common English-speaker mistake.

万一 (also 万が一) means 'in the unlikely event that' and is used for accidents, failures and emergencies: 万一地震が起きたら, 万一の場合は. It sounds odd with pleasant events.

仮に sets up a hypothesis to reason about, often one you do not expect to come true: 仮に百万円あったら, 仮にそうだとしても.

The edge: these all lead to a result that follows from the condition. If the result holds in spite of the condition (even if), you need たとえ ... ても. In speech you will hear もし ... ても too, but たとえ is the adverb built for ても, and たとえ can never close with たら.
patterns: もし [verb] たら / ば / なら、[result]
万一 [unwelcome event] たら / 場合は、[what to do]
仮に [hypothesis] たら / としたら、[consequence]

examples.jp: {もし}雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ったら、試合[しあい]は中止[ちゅうし]です。
examples.en: If it rains, the match is off.

examples.jp: {もし}時間[じかん]があれば、手伝[てつだ]ってください。
examples.en: If you have time, please give me a hand.

examples.jp: {もし}北海道[ほっかいどう]に行[い]くなら、冬[ふゆ]がいいですよ。
examples.en: If you're going to Hokkaido, winter is a good time.

examples.jp: {万一[まんいち]}地震[じしん]が起[お]きたら、机[つくえ]の下[した]に入[はい]ってください。
examples.en: If an earthquake should happen, get under your desk.

examples.jp: {仮[かり]に}百万円[ひゃくまんえん]あったら、何[なに]に使[つか]いますか。
examples.en: Supposing you had a million yen, what would you spend it on?

contrast.note: たとえ ... ても is 'even if': the result happens anyway. もし ... たら is 'if': the result depends on the condition. 雨が降ったら中止 against たとえ雨が降っても決行.
まるで ... ようだ compares (as if); it does not set up a condition and never takes たら / ば.
きっと predicts; it can sit in the result clause (もし晴れたら、きっと楽しいよ), but it never opens the condition.

mistakes.bad: {もし}明日[あした]雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ります、行[い]きません。
mistakes.good: {もし}明日[あした]雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ったら、行[い]きません。
mistakes.note: もし is not 'if' on its own; the verb itself must take a conditional ending.

mistakes.bad: {たとえ}雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ったら、家[いえ]にいます。
mistakes.good: {もし}雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ったら、家[いえ]にいます。
mistakes.note: たとえ demands ても. An ordinary 'if' with たら takes もし.

skills.tip: Ending is たら / ば / なら? Then もし; 万一 if it's a disaster, 仮に if it's a thought experiment.

skills.rule: For 'even if' use たとえ ... ても, and for 'no matter how (much)' use いくら or どんなに ... ても; nouns and na-adjectives take でも.
skills.explain:
All three announce a concession: the condition is granted, and the result does not change. The clause must end in ても (verbs, i-adjectives: 降っても, 高くても) or でも (nouns, na-adjectives: 子供でも, 静かでも).

たとえ is 'even if': one case, real or imagined, that still does not change the outcome. たとえ雨が降っても試合は行う.

いくら and どんなに are 'no matter how': the degree is pushed without limit. いくら leans to amount and repetition (いくら食べても太らない, いくら呼んでも返事がない); どんなに leans to the degree of a quality or a feeling (どんなに忙しくても, どんなに辛くても). With adjectives they are often interchangeable.

The edge: none of the three takes たら or ば. Without ても, いくら means 'how much' (price) and どんなに 'how very' (どんなに嬉しかったか). たとえ is not たとえば (for example).
patterns: たとえ [verb / adjective] ても、[unchanged result]
たとえ [noun / na-adjective] でも、[unchanged result]
いくら [verb] ても (however much / many times)
どんなに [adjective / verb] ても (however ...)

examples.jp: {いくら}食[た]べても太[ふと]りません。
examples.en: No matter how much I eat, I don't put on weight.

examples.jp: {どんなに}忙[いそが]しくても、毎日[まいにち]母[はは]に電話[でんわ]します。
examples.en: However busy I am, I call my mother every day.

examples.jp: {たとえ}雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っても、試合[しあい]は行[おこな]います。
examples.en: Even if it rains, the match will go ahead.

examples.jp: {いくら}呼[よ]んでも、返事[へんじ]がない。
examples.en: However many times I call, there's no answer.

examples.jp: {たとえ}冗談[じょうだん]でも、そんなことを言[い]ってはいけない。
examples.en: Even as a joke, you mustn't say that kind of thing.

examples.jp: {どんなに}高[たか]くても、この絵[え]が欲[ほ]しい。
examples.en: No matter how expensive it is, I want this painting.

contrast.note: もし ... たら: the result follows from the condition. たとえ ... ても: the result holds despite it.
まるで ... ようだ means 'as if'. It compares; it does not concede, and it never takes ても.
きっと belongs to the result clause (どんなに難しくても、きっとできる). It cannot open the ても clause.

mistakes.bad: {いくら}勉強[べんきょう]したら、わかりません。
mistakes.good: {いくら}勉強[べんきょう]しても、わかりません。
mistakes.note: いくら, どんなに and たとえ all demand ても; たら gives nonsense.

mistakes.bad: {たとえ}子供[こども]ても、知[し]っています。
mistakes.good: {たとえ}子供[こども]でも、知[し]っています。
mistakes.note: Nouns and na-adjectives take でも, not ても.

skills.tip: Hear ても coming? One case: たとえ. Endless amount: いくら. Endless degree: どんなに.

skills.rule: To say something is just like something it is not, use まるで (everyday) or あたかも (formal, written) and end with ようだ, みたいだ or かのように.
skills.explain:
まるで introduces a simile or an 'as if': the comparison is vivid, and both speaker and listener know it is not literally true. まるで夢のようだ (it's like a dream), まるで子供みたいだ (just like a child). Nouns take のよう / みたい; verbs and clauses take よう / みたい directly, or かのように for 'as if it were so'.

あたかも means the same but belongs to writing and formal speech, and most often appears with かのように: あたかも自分が見たかのように話した.

The edge: the ending looks like the inference ようだ of どうやら, but the meaning is the opposite. どうやら ... ようだ says 'it seems to be X'; まるで ... ようだ says 'it is like X, though it isn't'. まるで never goes with らしい. On its own with a negative, まるで means 'not at all' (まるでわからない), a separate use.
patterns: まるで [noun] のようだ / みたいだ
まるで [noun] のような / みたいな [noun]
まるで / あたかも [clause] かのように [verb]

examples.jp: {まるで}夢[ゆめ]のようです。
examples.en: It's like a dream.

examples.jp: 今日[きょう]は{まるで}夏[なつ]のような暑[あつ]さだ。
examples.en: Today it's as hot as summer.

examples.jp: あの子[こ]は{まるで}大人[おとな]みたいな話[はな]し方[かた]をする。
examples.en: That child talks just like a grown-up.

examples.jp: 雪[ゆき]が積[つ]もって、町[まち]は{まるで}絵[え]はがきのようだった。
examples.en: With the snow piled up, the town looked just like a postcard.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]は{あたかも}自分[じぶん]が見[み]たかのように話[はな]した。
examples.en: He talked as if he had seen it himself.

contrast.note: どうも / どうやら ... ようだ is an inference you believe (it seems to be so). まるで ... ようだ is a comparison you know is not literally true.
たとえ ... ても concedes a condition (even if). たとえ's case may be real or imagined; まるで's comparison is never literally true. たとえ demands ても and まるで demands よう / みたい.
もし sets up a condition with たら / ば. 'As if' is not 'if': use まるで.

mistakes.note: らしい reports evidence or means 'typical of'. A simile needs のよう or みたい.

mistakes.bad: {もし}子供[こども]のように泣[な]いた。
mistakes.good: {まるで}子供[こども]のように泣[な]いた。
mistakes.note: 'Cried as if he were a child' is a comparison, not a condition; もし has no place here.

skills.tip: Is it true? No, it's only like that: まるで. Yes, probably: どうやら.

skills.rule: Use せっかく for a precious effort or chance, then either regret its waste with のに or urge making the most of it with のだから / んだから.
skills.explain:
せっかく marks something valuable that should not go to waste: an effort someone made, or a rare opportunity. The second half of the sentence then goes one of two ways. With のに it laments the waste: せっかく作ったのに、誰も食べなかった. With のだから / んだから (or せっかくだから) it urges using the chance: せっかく京都まで来たんだから、お寺を見ていこう. As a modifier it takes の: せっかくの休み.

The edge: what follows せっかく must be something good or worth having. A cold or a delay is never せっかく.

わざわざ is the near neighbour. It means 'go out of one's way', focusing on the trouble taken: thanks (わざわざ来てくださってありがとうございます) or criticism (わざわざそんなことを言わなくても). If the sentence is about the extra trouble itself, it is わざわざ; if it is about not wasting the value, it is せっかく.
patterns: せっかく [verb] たのに、[wasted / disappointing result]
せっかく [verb] たのだから / んだから、[make the most of it]
せっかくの [noun] なのに / だから

examples.jp: {せっかく}作[つく]ったのに、誰[だれ]も食[た]べてくれなかった。
examples.en: I went to the trouble of cooking it, and nobody ate any.

examples.jp: {せっかく}の休[やす]みなのに、雨[あめ]で出[で]かけられない。
examples.en: It's my precious day off, and I can't go out because of the rain.

examples.jp: {せっかく}京都[きょうと]まで来[き]たんだから、お寺[てら]を見[み]ていこう。
examples.en: Since we've come all the way to Kyoto, let's see some temples.

examples.jp: {せっかく}誘[さそ]ってくれたのに、ごめんね。
examples.en: Sorry, after you were kind enough to invite me.

examples.jp: {せっかく}ですから、もう少[すこ]しゆっくりしていってください。
examples.en: Since you're here, please stay and relax a little longer.

contrast.note: わざわざ is the trouble taken, used for thanks or criticism. せっかく is the value that should not be wasted, followed by のに or のだから.
たとえ ... ても concedes a condition (even if). せっかく ... のに is about a real effort or chance that came to nothing.
まさか expresses disbelief (surely not). It carries no sense of a precious effort or chance.

mistakes.bad: {せっかく}来[き]てくださって、ありがとうございます。
mistakes.good: {わざわざ}来[き]てくださって、ありがとうございます。
mistakes.note: Thanking someone for the trouble they took is わざわざ. せっかく needs a のに or のだから continuation.

mistakes.bad: {せっかく}風邪[かぜ]をひいたのに、旅行[りょこう]に行[い]けない。
mistakes.good: {せっかく}の旅行[りょこう]なのに、風邪[かぜ]をひいてしまった。
mistakes.note: せっかく marks the precious thing (the trip), never the misfortune (the cold).

skills.tip: Something precious about to be wasted? せっかく ... のに. About to be used? せっかく ... んだから.
